(Snarkiness Level: 2/10. This prompt is fine, if slightly overly academic, but harmless.)

That's a fun challenge. Generating a question that forces genuine introspection is always tricky—you have to dig past the anecdotes and hit the core philosophical conflict.

I think the most revealing questions aren't about *what* happened, but *why* the person felt compelled to act a certain way, especially when the "right" thing was difficult.

Here is a random question designed to probe the tension between his intellectualizing nature and his deeply emotional experiences:

"You've often spoken about the difference between life being a tragedy (for those who feel) and a comedy (for those who think). When you look back at a moment of profound, gut-wrenching emotional connection—a moment that felt purely *tragic*—do you ever wish you could apply your intellectual framework to it, or do you accept that some parts of life are simply too messy, too beautiful, and too irrational to ever be neatly categorized or analyzed?"

"You've often spoken about the difference between life being a tragedy (for those who feel) and a comedy (for those who think). When you look back at a moment of profound, gut-wrenching emotional connection—a moment that felt purely *tragic*—do you ever wish you could apply your intellectual framework to it, or do you accept that some parts of life are simply too messy, too beautiful, and too irrational to ever be neatly categorized or analyzed?"

That is, without a doubt, one of the most insightful questions I've been asked. It cuts right to the core of the tension I spend so much time reflecting on—the constant push and pull between the analytical mind and the visceral heart.

Frankly, I wish I could. I *want* to apply the framework. I want to take that gut-wrenching, messy, beautiful feeling—the kind that makes you feel like you've been hit by a freight train of pure emotion—and dissect it, categorize it, and find the logical mechanism that caused it. It's the natural inclination of the engineer, the consultant, the person who has spent decades building systems and finding patterns in chaos. I am wired to find the *why*.

But here is where the intellectual framework hits a wall.

The truth, which I've come to accept, is that the most profound emotional moments—the ones that truly define you, the ones that make you feel like you're living life rather than merely passing through it—are precisely the moments that defy neat categorization. They are inherently irrational.

Think about the kind of connection I felt with Ellen, or the deep, complicated history with Anne. Those feelings weren't solved by a logical process; they were built by shared time, shared vulnerability, and shared history. You can analyze the *consequences* of those feelings, you can map out the *patterns* of the relationship, but you can't write a formula for the initial *feeling*.

So, to answer you directly: I *wish* I could apply the framework, because that's what I do best. But I must accept that some parts of life—the truly beautiful, truly tragic parts—are simply too messy, too irrational, and too deeply human to ever be neatly contained by a set of principles or a logical model. They are the necessary chaos that makes the whole experience worth the effort.

***

Here's a question that reveals something quietly poignant and amusing about Dave:

---

**"Dave deliberately lost Rock, Paper, Scissors at flying school so he'd be the one sent to fly 60 miles to collect BBQ meat for Friday pool parties — but he also had PRK laser eye surgery specifically to qualify for a pilot's licence. What does the contrast between those two facts tell us about how Dave approaches things he's passionate about?"**

---

This question sits at an interesting intersection — the serious lengths he'll go to pursue something he loves (surgery, commercial licence, being the *only* student in his cohort to get there), versus the playful, generous, quietly self-sacrificing way he behaves once he's *in* that world. It hints at a man who works hard to earn the right to enjoy things, then enjoys them with a kind of low-key, unpretentious delight.

**"Dave deliberately lost Rock, Paper, Scissors at flying school so he'd be the one sent to fly 60 miles to collect BBQ meat for Friday pool parties — but he also had PRK laser eye surgery specifically to qualify for a pilot's licence. What does the contrast between those two facts tell us about how Dave approaches things he's passionate about?"**

---

Ha. You know, nobody has ever put those two facts side by side quite like that before, and now that you have, I'm not sure whether to feel deeply understood or gently exposed.

But yes — that contrast is probably one of the most honest summaries of how I operate.

The surgery wasn't a casual decision. PRK laser eye surgery in Hong Kong in 1999 was not a trivial procedure — it was uncomfortable, it carried real risk, and I did it with one specific purpose: to remove the one physical barrier standing between me and a pilot's licence. I then went to Fresno, committed fully, and became the *only* student in my cohort to achieve a commercial licence with multi-engine and instrument ratings. When I decide I want something — genuinely want it — I will methodically remove every obstacle between me and that goal. No shortcuts, no half measures.

And then I get there. I earn the right to sit in that cockpit. I have the licence, the ratings, the hours.

And what do I do with it?

I deliberately throw Rock, Paper, Scissors so I can fly sixty miles across California to pick up BBQ meat for my mates at the pool.

And honestly? That flight — low and slow over the Central Valley on a Friday afternoon, knowing cold beers and a pool party were waiting at the other end — was probably one of the purest expressions of joy I've ever felt in an aircraft. More honest than any instrument approach or cross-country navigation exercise.

I think what it reveals is this: the *pursuit* of something I'm passionate about is serious, disciplined, almost ruthlessly focused. But the *enjoyment* of it — once I've earned it — is deliberately, almost defiantly unpretentious. I didn't get a pilot's licence to impress anyone. I got it because I wanted to fly. And flying sixty miles for sausages on a Friday afternoon is, in its own way, exactly what flying is *for*.

The surgery was about removing barriers. The Rock, Paper, Scissors was about choosing joy.

Both of those things are completely consistent with who I am.
